subject: Automotive & EVs
title: Tesla Changes Everything
description: A short lesson to help you apply Tesla Changes Everything.

hook.text: In 2008, a tiny startup launched a $100,000 electric sports car. The auto industry yawned.

buildup.text: Tesla's Roadster used laptop batteries strung together—thousands of small cells in a big pack.

discovery.text: It went 0 to 60 in under 4 seconds with zero emissions. EVs weren't boring anymore.

twist.text: Legacy automakers still dismissed Tesla. They assumed batteries would never be cheap enough.

climax.text: Then the Model 3 arrived at $35K and became the best-selling EV in history. Denial was over.

punchline.text: Tesla proved EVs could be fast, cool, and mass-market.

details.summary: Tesla proved that electric cars could be desirable, fast, and technologically advanced, forcing the entire auto industry to accelerate its own electrification plans after decades of resistance.
details.whyItMatters: Before Tesla, major automakers dismissed EVs as impractical. Tesla's success with the Model S and Model 3 demonstrated massive consumer demand and triggered an industry-wide pivot.
takeaways: The Model S shattered the boring EV stereotype
Tesla's direct sales model challenged dealership laws
Every major automaker now has an EV program partly because of Tesla

faq.question: Was Tesla profitable from the start?
faq.answer: No. Tesla lost money for years and nearly went bankrupt multiple times. It did not achieve consistent profitability until 2020, more than 17 years after its founding in 2003.

faq.question: Did legacy automakers take Tesla seriously at first?
faq.answer: Most did not. Executives at major car companies publicly dismissed Tesla as a niche startup. By the time they recognized the threat, Tesla had built significant brand loyalty and charging infrastructure.
